routes.description: The available evidence makes belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God irrational because apparently gratuitous evil conflicts with that God, salvation is perilously unclear, and major appeals to God as an explanation face naturalistic alternatives or grounding dilemmas.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the stated counterevidence or objections make belief in the specified God insufficiently supported by the reason and evidence available to a believer.

bridges.description: Given the available reason and evidence, belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God is irrational.
Apparently gratuitous suffering is incompatible with an all-powerful, all-loving God and remains decisive counterevidence even if arguments for a generic creator are granted.
Making grave or eternal outcomes depend on salvation beliefs whose requirements are disputed and culturally inaccessible conflicts with an all-loving God.
Evolution can select broadly reliable cognition because systematically false beliefs are costly, so human rationality does not require divine guidance.
Divine moral grounding fails because goodness is either independent of God or defined by God arbitrarily, and identifying God with goodness merely restates the dilemma.

routes.description: Belief in God is rational because God provides a cumulative explanation of trustworthy reason, cosmic fine-tuning, and objective morality, while suffering is serious counterevidence but not a defeater.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if these features are more expected or intelligible given God than without God and the available responses prevent evil from defeating the resulting cumulative case.

bridges.description: Given the available reason and evidence, belief in God is rational.
The cumulative explanatory force of reason, fine-tuning, and objective morality makes God more probable than nonexistence, while evil remains nondefeating counterevidence.
Unguided evolution selects primarily for survival rather than truth, whereas an intelligent creator supplies a rational basis for trusting human minds.
The universe's life-permitting fine-tuning is extraordinarily improbable by chance and therefore supports an intelligent designer.
Objective moral obligations are difficult to ground in an impersonal universe and are best grounded in God as the personal source of goodness.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: An all-powerful God can prevent evil and an all-loving God wants to prevent it, yet mass extinctions, disease, predation, and other apparently purposeless suffering indicate gratuitous evil that such a God cannot admit.
moves.attributionBasis: The span occurs within Woodford's uninterrupted opening case after the moderator explicitly hands him the floor, and it addresses Simon by name from Woodford's stated position.
moves.selectionRationale: This 132-word first-quartile span contains one bounded inference from divine power and love plus observed purposeless suffering to the incompatibility asserted by the pro central bridge.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Many theists make salvation necessary to avoid annihilation or eternal torment, yet Christians, Muslims, and Jews disagree about the beliefs required for salvation.
moves.attributionBasis: The span remains inside Woodford's uninterrupted opening presentation and follows his explicit introduction of soteriological confusion.
moves.selectionRationale: This 162-word first-quartile span isolates the salvation-confusion argument and supplies the disputed requirements and severe consequences needed to recover its single inferential role.

moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: Life-permitting physical parameters occupy an extraordinarily narrow range, making their occurrence by chance practically impossible and indicating that a superintellect arranged the universe.
moves.attributionBasis: The span is part of Edwards's uninterrupted three-argument opening case, explicitly introduced as his design argument after the moderator hands him the floor.
moves.selectionRationale: This 176-word second-quartile span preserves the probability comparison, life-permitting consequence, and designer inference as one atomic fine-tuning argument.

moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: Taken cumulatively, the arguments from rationality, teleology, and morality make God's existence more probable than nonexistence and belief in God more rational than the alternative.
moves.attributionBasis: This is Edwards's explicit conclusion to his uninterrupted opening presentation, immediately before he thanks the audience and the moderator resumes.
moves.selectionRationale: This 78-word second-quartile span expressly states the complete motion-level conclusion rather than merely repeating one supporting example.

moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: Edwards personally confronted apparently unnecessary suffering while watching his grandmother die after an accident and, as a Christian, cried out to ask why God allowed it.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly directs the problem-of-evil question to Edwards immediately before this first-person account, and the speaker identifies himself as a Christian during it.
moves.selectionRationale: This 117-word third-quartile span is an important first-person acknowledgment of suffering but does not itself supply a reason that any stated bridge is true or false.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: The prevalence of atheism among philosophers and those who study religion, together with rising atheism, irreligiosity, and secularism, undercuts a narrative of resurgent faith.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator has handed the response to Woodford, and this span continues his uninterrupted first-person reply challenging Edwards's appeal to philosophers.
moves.selectionRationale: This 133-word third-quartile span makes a recoverable demographic argument about intellectual and social trends, but that proposition can be true without altering any route bridge.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Even granting every argument for a creator, the world's evil prevents identifying that creator with the all-powerful, all-loving Christian God or Allah.
moves.attributionBasis: The span directly continues Woodford's uninterrupted response and explicitly returns to the problem of evil he says he raised in his opening.
moves.selectionRationale: This 136-word third-quartile span grants the con route's positive arguments for purposes of rebuttal and directly denies that their cumulative conclusion survives the counterevidence from evil.

moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: The Euthyphro dilemma is answered because God neither follows an independent good nor makes goodness arbitrary; God is goodness itself and is the personal source in which objective goodness is rooted.
moves.attributionBasis: Woodford has just posed the dilemma directly to Edwards, and this span is Edwards's explicit answer, framed from his own position and referring back to Woodford's formulation.
moves.selectionRationale: This 158-word fourth-quartile span directly rejects both horns of the pro divine-grounding objection and offers Edwards's single alternative grounding proposition.
